h:
They will come to you with charts.

Clean lines trending upward.

Violent crime down 11 %.

GDP growth 2.7 %.

Global life expectancy at record highs.

Average daily screen time 8.4 hours.

Marvel Cinematic Universe gross: $29.8 billion and counting.

They will present these numbers the way high priests once presented entrails:

Behold, the omens are favorable.

The gods of progress are pleased.

Do not argue with the numbers.

The numbers are usually accurate.

That is precisely how the spirit works.

Babylon never needs to falsify the data.

It only needs to persuade you that the data is the story.

A city can have the lowest homicide rate in fifty years and still feel like a tomb because no one trusts his neighbor, no child plays unsupervised, and every porch light is armed.

A nation can post record GDP while its young men post record despair, its birth rate collapses, and its churches become coffee shops.

A boy can log eight hundred hours in a single season and emerge more hollow than when he began, because the game was engineered never to let him finish anything that matters.

The dashboard cannot measure what was never entered into the spreadsheet.

It cannot measure the silence where hymns used to be.

It cannot measure the weight of a father’s absence or the absence of weight in a father who is physically present but spiritually gone.

It cannot measure the moment a story stops moving the soul and starts moving product.

It cannot measure the exact second a people trades memory for stimuli.

These things leave no forensic trace in the official statistics.

They leave only the quiet ache you have learned to call “normal.”

The priests of the dashboard will call you nostalgic, irrational, ungrateful.

They will ask for your alternative metric.

They will demand a counter-spreadsheet.

Give them none.

Some things are measured only by the heart that has been trained to finish what it starts, to mourn what has been lost, to recognize what the dashboard can never see.

The dashboard is not malicious.

It is merely blind.

And blindness at highway speed is a kind of malice all its own.

We do not need better numbers.

We need better questions.

Not “How much?”

But “To what end?”

Not “How long?”

But “Toward what telos?”

Not “How efficient?”

But “How faithful?”

Until we ask those questions again, every upward tick on the dashboard is only a more precise measurement of how elegantly the corpse has been embalmed.

The numbers are correct.

The story is over.

Kingdom Code continues the autopsy.

The dashboard’s blindness isn’t accidental. It’s the same mechanism that turned entertainment from a source of transformation into a tool of extraction. Games that never end. Movies that never resolve. Music that never lasts. All of it designed to keep you scrolling, consuming, and numbed, while the numbers tick upward and the soul ticks downward.
